analysis_text: Katana Zero was an incredible experience from start to finish. The pixel art and visual style are absolutely gorgeous. Every level is full of personality, and the neon aesthetic makes the game look incredibly stylish. It's certainly not another MetroVania Flop. The story was the biggest surprise for me. I expected a fun action game, but I ended up completely invested in the characters and the mystery. The gameplay is fast, satisfying, an rewards precision. Finally pulling off a perfect run after figuring everything out felt amazing. The soundtrack ties everything toghether perfectly. Overall, this is one of those games that'll stay a while after the credits roll. If you enjoy stylish action games with a great story and gameplay that rewards skill, this game is absolutely worth playing.

title: Small Saga
analysis_text: Small Saga was pretty mediocre. There are some pretty cute moments where I enjoyed the characters and how they reacted to the events unfolding. However, the overall story operates at so much of a breakneck pace that it makes character development incredibly jarring; characters will flip motivation on a dime just to railroad the main plot. In the span of ~6 hours, you [spoiler] help a child run away from home, start a prison break which leads to overthrowing an authoritarian town and installing a new leader, start a revolution against the monarchy, overthrow a slaver, and help a person reconcile their past[/spoiler]. The game honestly tries to do too much too fast, which makes transitioning between main story beats turbulent. This results in characters not realistically offering pushback on others or having instantaneous changes of heart. Simultaneously, new ideas and information on people’s past are constantly introduced, but never meaningfully utilized or elaborated on. Many of the main story conflicts are resolved off screen and are only barely mentioned being resolved in a few sentences. A few characters are particularly loathsome with cringy dialogue in the form of forced memes. There are also several references to memes that were topical at the time. Constant attempts at humor are made but they mostly fall flat. The story takes up the vast majority of the game with some light amount of boss combat near the climax of each plot point. The combat is extremely vapid to the point it feels like a fantasy story masquerading as an RPG. There aren’t any meaningful decisions to make in terms of building character skills or gear. In fact, the game has several skills that increase damage to different types of enemies that either appear in only 2 combats or only in one chapter. I never felt in danger during combat and it boiled down to spamming damage abilities with no thought. It is very dissonant to be a meek rodent trying to rise up against larger creatures while combat is never dangerous. The final boss of the game was doing attacks that did 2 damage to me. There is a lack of polish that hampers the storytelling experience. Many important story moments had no music or ambient sound that made reading the dialogue emotionally hollow. Nearly every cutscene in the game used fades to black to hide actions being performed, items being placed, etc. There are also many incredibly long walkways between story areas that don’t serve any purpose to gameplay or storytelling. They don’t build atmosphere and just pad playtime as you meander through empty halls in dead silence. Overall, I found Small Saga to be entertaining enough to want to see the game through. The game was gifted to me and I think if I had spent the $15 myself, I would be more disappointed. For that reason, I can’t really recommend this game to others for its price. The plot is too hasty and needs to take more time so that many of the introduced threads are not hand waved away.

title: Small Saga
analysis_text: [h2]I'm Ashamed I Forgot About This Gem![/h2] You know that feeling of once playing through something fantastic, something that gave it its all with strong visual identity, memorable characters, and a story that genuinely sticks, only for it to slowly fade into the back of your mind years later? Well... I know that feeling well. That’s Small Saga. A JRPG that proves you do not need a massive open world to sell the idea of an incredible RPG. As even the smallest creatures have a big story to tell. [h2]Issue[/h2] Small Saga’s biggest issue was it's visibility. It released quietly and never quite got the spotlight it deserved, releasing around the same time that huge RPGs like (Baldurs Gate 3) were gaining traction. This of course made it easy to overlook or forget entirely. On top of that, I would have to say that a lot of people just don't like the idea of a linear RPG, you know, like myself. I prefer to overlevel and overexplore until I am a god, but here it's all on the rails story progression. Pacing can also feel somewhat quick, leaving some moments you wish had more time to breathe and fully come to life, but that's more on the small side. [h2]Impression[/h2] At its core, this is a classic JRPG. You manage a traditional party setup with a healer, support, and two fighters with some debuffs and buffs to help you on your journey. Progression is tied to boss fights, with a level gained after each one. For some players, this is where the experience can feel overly streamlined and, at times, unfun when you can't power level. This is similar to how a game like Chained Echoes handled progression, which was not fun. Combat itself is rarely challenging as long as you lean into the game’s powerful combo effects, which can make most encounters trivial. That lack of difficulty may leave some players underwhelmed. Where the game truly stands apart is its story, which is genuinely amazing. This is elevated even further by the pixelated, cinematic presentation during boss fights and key story moments. Those sequences are striking and memorable, and they do a lot of heavy lifting in setting the game apart from others in the genre. It's a solo developed masterpiece in every possible way. [h2]Story[/h2] You play as a small mouse in a vast, dangerous world. After your brother is killed by the Yellow God, you swear revenge and set out to end this particular humans tyranny. With your life destroyed, the rodent population of Rodentia lives in fear, until you march into the den of beasts on a quest far larger than you could realistically handle alone. Along the way, you grow stronger, learning from allies and experiences, as your journey shapes not only Verm, the sole survivor of the Yellow God’s reign, but also the other characters you encounter. The story emphasizes growth, resilience, and the bonds formed in the face of overwhelming odds, giving the narrative depth beyond the typical revenge tale. It's surprisingly emotional, and for once again a mostly solo-developed title, this is one such game you don't want to miss out on for various reasons. It's one of the best of it's kind. [h2]Conclusion[/h2] I’ve played through this game once and am now finishing a second full playthrough. I had completely forgotten how good it truly was. That’s the thing with games like this: no matter how memorable they were, over the years the impact of the story, character development, and world-building can gradually fade, but returning to them is like starting over fresh. You get to re-experience the joys of this world and appreciate for what it offers. Then one day, you decide to give it another try, expecting little more than a dull story because you personally feel bored of all the other games you have or haven't played, and suddenly you’re completely absorbed, hooked by the story, invested in the characters, and captivated by the presentation. So do yourself a favor: take a deep breath, stop hesitating, and pick up Small Saga. It’s an experience you won’t soon forget, unless you well... Forget like I did, over time. title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: Ikenfell is a sweet little RPG I do like the game; the music is good, the story is nice. The gameplay left a bit to be desired, though. I found later-game activity to be rather frustrating and I ended up turning on easy mode; the two main grievances I have are routinely getting screwed over by the enemy party having too many turns in a row, and some actions, such as placing traps, not counting as a turn at all unless you do it. The last few sections of the game were so frustrating to me that they ended up souring the game in general a bit. I can't hold it against it too much, though: I'm not great at RPGs, and I don't like them much. Unfortunately many of the really good indie games seem to be RPGs. I'm not over the moon about this game but it's pretty good and probably worth your time, especially if you like this sort of game.

title: Ikenfell

analysis_text: So nice I bought it twice. After finishing the base game and DLC on PlayStation I decided it was time to move to some better hardware. Don't let the 7 hours playtime fool you, I've sunk at least 1,000 hours into this game. What can I say about this game that hasn't already been said a million times? This game is an undeniable masterpiece. The culmination of expert narrative construction, environmental storytelling and lore, awe inspiring vistas, mind blowing architecture, unparalleled gameplay, perfect sound design, epic score, staggering enemy variety including some of the coolest bosses in any FromSoft game to date with some of the most fascinating backstories and relationships. Not to mention an unbelievable amount of weapons, spells and armour to choose from to customise your Tarnished to your liking. The Soulsborne series has always been about overcoming adversity, and I don't think that's more present than in this game. It is genuinely overwhelming the sense of wonder and triumph this game provides, even on multiple playthroughs. I only wish I was legitimately at the 7 hour play time mark, I would love to go back and experience this all from the very beginning again, and again, and again... ad infinitum... Thank you Miyazaki and team, truly.

title: Finding Paradise
analysis_text: Great follow-up to To the Moon and another reminder that I really love these playable novel type games. What makes this one so fun is the mix of mystery and banter. I was always curious about what was really going on, what we were about to learn, and where the story was heading next. That kept me hooked the whole way through. At the same time, Dr. Watts and Dr. Rosalene make everything entertaining scene by scene, and Watts especially was a huge part of the fun for me with all his sarcasm, jokes, and random references. The low-friction interaction helps too, because the game stays focused on what it does best. The music and atmosphere were excellent! Now I’m really looking forward to Impostor Factory. I feel so lucky getting to play these all at once given these games originally came out years apart!

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: This is the second-to-last game in the [i]To the Moon[/i] series. As with the previous titles, you can expect gorgeous pixel art, a beautiful soundtrack, expressive animations, and a lot of reading. Fortunately, the writing is top-notch. It leans far more toward a walking simulator than a traditional video game. In fact, Impostor Factory features even less player interaction than its predecessors. There are no more puzzles here at all. Instead, it focuses almost entirely on delivering its narrative. It is difficult for me to say which of the three main games I have liked the most so far. However, I can definitely say that Impostor Factory was the most emotionally impactful for me. The plot remained gripping all the way to the end, and the post-credits scene leaves plenty of room for speculation. I am glad there is still one more game left for me to play in this series. I guess I am just a sucker for these short, narrative-driven pixel art games.

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: While some critics have pointed out that the story did not live to its "true potential", I personally think that for what it is; a story about finding meaning in an artificial world, it delivers its intended message exceptionally well. Impostor Factory doesn't need to be a complex sci-fi epic to be brilliant. It shows us that a physical reality doesn't really matter all that much. If you are feeling genuine love, grief or joy, then those emotions are 100% real to you in that moment. It's honestly my favorite so far from the series.

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: Another game in the now long-running To the Moon series, Impostor Factory has so many twists and turns that they're becoming the hallmark of the entire series. [spoiler] And to think that a simple murder mystery leads to the actual origins episode for the entire series, detailing how Neil Watts existed in the first place. [/spoiler] Looks like I'll look forward to the beach episode, which is stated to be the penultimate game in the series.

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: Impostor Factory is interesting in that it challenges the philosophy presented in the previous games and sets up the Beach Episode for success by starting to put the hypocritical actions and beliefs of characters front and center. Also, compared to the other games, it also seems to focus a lot more closely on the emotions of the characters without them having to explicitly state how they were feeling. Characters cry and don't need to state why exactly they cry. You just know. I could notice that Kan Gao was making a clear effort to improve his writing and storytelling within Impostor Factory and, even if it isn't perfect, it still tells a cohesive story that can be enjoyed on its own. I also feel the need to pay some respects to Jordan Baer as this was the last game of the series that he was directly involved in (funny that his last game was very focused on being caught between living a normal life or a life dedicated to lighting the way for others). I hope his family is doing alright.

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: Impostor Factory is significantly different to the first two To the Moon games, and it suffers for it. Unfortunately, I would consider this one to be the weakest of the series. To be clear, it is not a bad game, and it fits as an integral piece of the whole, but the level of captivation the other games manage in me is not quite achieved. I believe this is due to the change in protagonist, as Neil and Eva have next to no presence in the bulk of the story. They were what made the other games pop, with their funny, charming dialogue contrasting with the emotional weight of the others' stories, a sort of 'chiaroscuro' effect, if you will, that was incredible. As a part of the series, this is a must-play, but on its own, it has much to be desired. 6/10

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: If you enjoy other games from this developer, you will probably enjoy Impostor Factory. It has the same emotional heart-tugging, sense of jokiness, and "real/not-real?" memory happenings. It has the same flawed characters doing things, unspecified "medical condition", and people telling you there's a big secret that they're keeping but they can't tell you what the secret is. It's difficult for me to rate this game strictly "recommended" or "not recommended" but I'll flag it as recommended since it's better than the vast majority of games I've played. I give Impostor Factory a 7 out of 10.

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: [b]Impostor Factory[/b] serves as the missing link that finally brings the SigCorp saga together. While initially presented as a standalone murder mystery, it slowly reveals itself as a deeply connected narrative that ties [i]To the Moon[/i], [i]Finding Paradise[/i], and the minisodes into a single, coherent whole. What begins as an intriguing game gradually transforms into one of Kan Gao's most confident and emotionally resonant stories. Narratively, Impostor Factory feels like a return to form. The main theme is just as approachable as [i]Finding Paradise[/i] while having the same finesse in storytelling as [i]To the Moon[/i], taking the best of both worlds. The central twist was genuinely unpredictable to me, yet completely logical in hindsight, which is a very difficult balance to strike. The game also manages to expand [spoiler]Neil[/spoiler] as a character: questions that lingered across previous entries are addressed, adding layers of depth that recontextualize his behavior throughout the series. Overall, Impostor Factory feels like the perfect conclusion to a theoretical trilogy. It respects the legacy of the previous games while standing on its own, delivering one of the strongest narrative experiences in the series. [h1]The Good[/h1] + Perfectly ties together [i]To the Moon[/i], [i]Finding Paradise[/i], and the minisodes + Adds significant depth to [spoiler]Neil[/spoiler] and answers long-standing questions about him + Feels like a natural and satisfying conclusion to the trilogy + Storytelling is top tier, easily the strongest aspect of the game + Soundtrack and ambience are once again flawless + Plot twist manages to be the central piece that ties everything together while still being surprising + Baited by Kan Gao by thinking this was just a "murder mystery thriller featuring multiple casualties", unrelated to the past games + Still using the greatest game engine of all time, RPG Maker, to its full potential + We can finally run!! [h1]The Bad[/h1] - None. Well played. (first game I review where I have zero complaints, quite an achievement!) [i]Is it wrong if all I really wanted to be is just another lavender?[/i] [h2]10 / 10 - IGN[/h2]

analysis_text: To the Moon is a story-driven point-and-click adventure with charming pixelated visuals and short length. I also enjoyed the extra minisodes; while they're not nearly as emotionally impactful or thematically rich as the main game, they further develop some characters and bridge the story to the later entries in the series. title: To the Moon
analysis_text: This is a short and fun game. Although I went in expecting a very good story, I found exactly that… but it was even better constructed than I had expected. “To The Moon” is very light and easy to play. It is fun and relaxing. The fact that it is a short game also keeps it from feeling repetitive. The game just feels right. The gameplay is very simple. You only have to walk, listen to dialogues, and find memories throughout the scenes… and that is basically it. Yes, you have to solve a puzzle every time you change memories, but they are so easy that I would not categorize the game as a puzzle game. There is no combat, except for one brief section, the exploration is good (even though the game is linear), and, for me, the only two bugs I encountered were related to the game's only achievement and with a word writing puzzle. The solution for this last one was to launch the game in the classic version. The only achievement is awarded for beating the game, but after I finished it, I did not unlock it. The solution was to follow a guide on how to get it, and in less than 10 minutes everything was working properly. If you like short, relaxing games with a great soundtrack and a good story, you should definitely give it a try.

analysis_text: I'm not sure why exactly I'm always hesitant to play through Finding Paradise when I go through the whole series. It could be that it's the longest entry and kind of suffers from dragging a bit in a few places compared to the extremely tight pacing of To The Moon. It could also be that I don't connect as much with Colin as I do with Johnny (of course this could change with time.) It could even be that the funny banter between Neil and Eva somewhat breaks the pacing more in this entry compared to To The Moon. Even if it is a weaker entry, Finding Paradise will still find a way to make you cry and question your own existence and relationships. It might even give you a whole new way to look at your own reality. Who knows? It's the perfect opposite side of the coin to To The Moon in more ways than one.

title: Finding Paradise
analysis_text: 9/10, subtracted 1 because I couldn't find paradise. (Kidding, of course. I really like the game.) The people who worked on this lovely little gem throw the concept of a genre around like a hot potato. That isn't a bad thing, mind you; I find it amusing and effective. One moment I'm laughing at Neil and Eva's usual banter, then the next I'm feeling uneasy because... well, I'm not here to spoil anything. But if you liked To the Moon and want to see what other funny and emotionally heavy shenanigans the scientists get up to, I recommend checking this game out. The little details such as characters' background actions, along with how expressive everyone is, seemed to improve a lot here. I loved the sprite work. It felt like the world I was watching was really alive. I thought the game wouldn't affect me as much as TtM did, so I really didn't expect to be so invested that I ignored all my plans for the day just to finish it. It packed a punch in more ways than one and made me rethink some aspects of my life. Just the music playing when I saw the title screen for the first time was enough to make me realize I was in for an interesting ride. I find it funny how the new client and his wife are also musically inclined, though. Are all musicians bound to have bittersweet lives? Should I be concerned...?

title: Finding Paradise
analysis_text: I finished Finding Paradise in about 5 hours of gameplay, and the experience felt like gently walking through someone else’s memories. The game tells an emotional story focused on life, choices, and unspoken feelings, relying on strong writing and a beautiful soundtrack rather than complex gameplay. Its narrative unfolds slowly and quietly, allowing each moment to settle and giving weight to even the smallest details. The gameplay is simple and exists mainly to support the story, with light puzzles and exploration guiding you through different memories. What stayed with me was not what I did, but what I felt along the way — moments of warmth, sadness, and reflection that felt very human. I enjoyed the experience so much that I ended up finishing the game again afterward, letting the story sink in even deeper. Finding Paradise is a short but heartfelt journey that lingers long after it ends.

title: Finding Paradise
analysis_text: Finding Paradise is the sequel to the game that broke my heart, and while it didn't have that particle lightning-in-a-bottle effect on me, that is not because I think the game is worse. Part of the shock of To the Moon to me was how much I personally related to it, and that I was not expecting it to be so deeply emotional. I expected something similar from Finding Paradise, and on that it does succeed. This game does everything you would want from a sequel for To the Moon. It gives us another heartbreaking life to relive and expands on the formula. Whereas previously we went back in time, seeing a love story in reverse to try and figure out what the hell is going on in this guy's memories, we instead see a beginning and an ending that seem impossible to reconcile, with similarly heartbreaking reveals as we try and figure out what the hell is wrong with this guy's memories. It also manages to inject some real tension and more character moments for our Sigmund crew. Despite knowing how the memory gimmick works, finding paradise manages to keep the framing device fresh, and even expands on it from the first game. Play it anyway. It isn't quite as bittersweet as the first game, but it is still incredibly bittersweet. It hurts, it really does. If you liked the first one, play this one.

analysis_text: [h1]In Stars In Time (or Your Guidebook To Creating Insipid Internet-Brained Mediocrity!)[/h1] In Stars And Time by insertdisc5 and published by Armor Game Studios in November 2023 is a game of utter friction, some deliberate, some clearly much less so. The game follows Siffrin, a one-eyed rogue stuck in a time loop, and his party of four other companions: Mirabelle, Bonnie, Odile and Isabeau. Together you’re trying to save the country of Vaugarde from the malaise of the mysterious “[spoiler]King[/spoiler]”, whose mysterious time corruption magic is freezing everyone in the country in place, literally stopping them in time. You (as Siffrin) need to use your wits to bring the [spoiler]King[/spoiler]’s reign of terror to an end and rescue Vaugarde and your friends, no matter how many loops it takes! This game is insipid and the overwhelmingly positive reviews boggle my mind and here is why ---------------------------------------------------------------------- [h3]The highly restrictive word count of Steam's review system didn't allow me to express my full thoughts, so here's the full review on [url=https://infinitebacklog.net/users/indietail/reviews/in-stars-and-time]Infinite Backlog[/url] or on [url=https://medium.com/@indietails/in-stars-in-time-and-you-fe9fc16a3b97?sharedUserId=indietails]Medium[/url] (this version has pictures, extra criticism and jokes) [/h3]

title: In Stars And Time
analysis_text: I think this game was amazing. The art is great, the story compelling (i couldn't stop playing it until i was finished even though I was in the middle of uni exams), the music got stuck in my head(although it tends to repeat...), but the thing that made me LOVE this game were the characters. Every dialogue felt real, the main cast all felt like fleshed out people who existed outside of the cutscenes, with their own problems and little worlds. They even all have different religions which I was compelled by. Siffirin's breakdown was so immersive and raw, partly because we both shared the frustration of having to go through the whole game over and over and over again (the battles felt tedious quickly but I just pushed through it, just as siffirin had to). The dynamics between the main cast were heartwarming and cozy and fleshed out the characters even more. It's one of the sweetest found families I've seen :] I think this game is underrated and you should play it!

[spoiler]mirabelle's concerns about romance, odile's thoughts about her home and the childhood she missed out on, bonnie's fears and confusion about being cared for, isa's need to change and his lovely view of his old self.[/spoiler] i understood what they all meant and it was both a punch in the face and a warm hug. so many of these dialogues felt like real conversations ive had, and should have. siffrin is so tragic and so very special to me, i relate to his wish. i understand his loneliness, i understand his issues with his memory, i get it. title: In Stars And Time
analysis_text: This is an incredibly underrated game that is almost impossible to put down once you start it. There's nothing I would change about it at all. What stands out the most to me are the characters; they're very believable and their dialogue feels like how real-life people talk. Side characters are also interesting to talk to and are memorable and worth engaging with. The character art is great as well, with many different nuanced and detailed art works, portraits and expressions for the main character (Siffrin) and their friends. What was impressive to me was how the game has a very mature and realistic portrayal of mental health struggles. Siffrin's reactions to the time loops are very relatable, as was much of his internal dialogue throughout the game. I really felt bad for them as the story progressed. The game doesn't shy away from dark topics, and approaches them in a way that doesn't downplay their impact. The time loops themselves are handled perfectly. They don't get (that) tedious due to the various ways you can skip dialogue, areas, or get around certain repetitive tasks. You can always ask a character for help too if you're stuck, and fights get faster and optionally avoidable too the more loops you go through. The combat in general is fun and engaging. I was never bored and enjoyed it until the very end. I had so much fun with In Stars And Time and cannot recommend it enough. Absolutely worth playing AND replaying for all the secrets you can find everywhere.

title: In Stars And Time
analysis_text: I just finished this game and I can not understate how AMAZING the story is. Although I knew how the ending would go by the midpoint of the story, they journey and catharsis of seeing how it was done made it more than worth it. The main message that I gathered from the story has changed my perspective in life in a way that can never be undone. The characters are all delightful, with their own charms and struggles that make them relatable. Siffrin makes a great user character with his silly puns and clear identity. His ideas and thoughts progress changes throughout the story is realistic in a way that hit close to home for me and likely many other people. The dialogue can be very silly and funny, especially when hearing it for the first time. But some conversations had me crying, reflecting on my own life choices. As you continue through the game, some of the dialogue can get tiring to hear over and over again but I think that is an important part of the experience (and there is a skip feature for a reason). I enjoyed seeing how Siffrin's answers to questions did (or didn't) change a characters reaction. I will not lie, some parts of the game can drag, especially if you were to get lost in the loops. Although the game does have enough help in the form of Loop, it can still be a bit confusing to find out how to progress. I did have to look up a guide but I think it's just because I wasn't paying enough attention. It did add a bit more realism to the reason behind Siffrin's actions but I can understand why some players may not enjoy it. What made the game easy to play was the amazing soundtrack and cute artstyle. This OST is played constantly at my work when I have control of the music, lol. And the visuals are clean, cute and simple. Simple changes to Siffrin's sprites throughout the game play make it easier to keep looping since there's something new to see. The emotions in each art work can be seen so clearly. Overall, a truly amazing game that was crafted with love and deserves so much more recognition.

title: In Stars And Time
analysis_text: Playing this game was an experience I will never forget! :D The art and music draws you in, but the comradery between Isabeau, Odile, Mirabelle, Bonnie, and Siffrin as well as the twists and turns along the way keep you locked in. I had so much fun just reading the dialogue between characters. So much humor and charm behind nearly every interaction, even with the people in the town. Their friendship is an anchor in a world of chaos, and it's so wholesome despite the pressure they faced. I also liked how the battle system was based on rock. paper, scissors, even if it did make combat less complex as a turn-based game. My only gripe with the battle system was how tedious it became to battle over the course of the game. I eventually found an item that allowed me to circumvent some of the tediousness which was nice. My main complaint with the game is that there are certain parts that feel unnecessarily frustrating and difficult to complete. I would say Act 4 gave me the most trouble and I actually had to go through a walkthrough twice in order to finally pass it. The story, characters, art, and music make it worth it but it does feel a little too much at certain points even if I understand it relates to a core part of the story. I highly recommend this game! This is one of those games that can change your life by playing. I will never forget my buddies Siffrin, Odile, Isabeau, Mirabelle, and Bonnie ; u; <3

title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: (Note: I left it running in the background a lot which is why there's so many hours on it) Final Thoughts: It's not *great*, but it's still pretty good, except the pacing never picks up the way it feels like it should. Combat starts off fun and interesting as you learn the mechanics, but it never really gets more difficult or complex, there's just *more* of it, and the addition of traps and a few other things that keep the pacing slow left me wanting to just skip combat after a while except for the boss fights, and even then it was really just to see if I could steal some unique loot from them or see if they had any wacky mechanics to them. The story is... weirdly enough, kind of the same way. It's never *bad*, and if you like stories about magic schools and have an aching void in your life because you can't look at Harry Potter the same way anymore, this isn't a bad way to fill it. It's just that the journey to get to it becomes kind of cyclical: go to new place, fight some monsters, get a teeny bit of lore, and now if you want to know more you need this new McGuffin or talk to this other person whom no one thought to talk to prior so now we go to a new area and do it all over again. The whole thing is about 20-25 hours long, and somewhere around the halfway mark I started feeling like I just wanted to get to the end so I could have all of the mysteries unraveled and find out what actually was going on and how it turns out. So yeah, turned on Combat Skipping and just played out fights when I felt like it, and at that point it started to be fun again because the pacing sped up a lot and I was able to get through the rest of the story. Again, not a *great* story, but pretty good. All in all, it's worth playing if either the premise of young adult magic stories or timed tactical RPG intrigued you, although you'll probably want to tweak the settings at some point unless you just REALLY can't get enough of that combat, in which case, have at it I guess :)

title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: I'm sad to give this a negative review but as the game went on, it only got worse and worse until I couldn't take the game seriously anymore. The cast is entirely queer, including one person with neopronouns which is nice to see. The story and characters are generally very shallow, and around the midpoint of the game each chapter starts feeling monotonous as the plot takes too many twists and turns to have been planned out beforehand. Combat is generally enjoyable, though in the late game health pools start scaling up and it's hard not to want a defensive build when a couple bad timings could cost 3/4 of a party member's health bar. Assigning equipment is rather unwieldy, as there's too many choices that are hard to compare to each other and become obsolete every other chapter, as well as completely arbitrary weapon upgrades that are just a money sink. There's adequate accessibility options to both autocomplete action commands as well as fights themselves, and also an option to display content warnings which is very much appreciated. The ending solidified my negative review. No specifics, but [spoiler] after defeating what you'd think to be the final boss, another character unleashes barely-hinted at powers and you have to slog through a whole other multi-phase boss fight with them that I guess is supposed to be sad? the music in the fight is orchestral and somber but it's a full encounter that's only a little lower in difficulty compared to the previous boss. it's just baffling how the pace could be killed THAT quickly. [/spoiler] to its credit, the music is very good, though I think playing songs with lyrics during some boss fights was a mistake. it's undoubtedly the best part of the game, alongside the charming pixel art graphics. if you do play ikenfell, feel free to spin the control stick around in battle to fly into the sky!!

title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: tl;dr -- The storytelling and the soundtrack are pretty good. The gameplay falls off quickly, starting from the mid-game. Early game is balanced well and enjoyable. Chapter boss HP scales exponentially and their damage scales linearly. Your damage from levels and your damage from gear scale VERY linearly. Which means your damage will get outpaced starting from the mid-game. Late game, the bosses start to hit you for 45-80% of your HP while you will hit them for 3-4% of their HP: If you build damage, you deal 4% and take 80-100% of your HP per boss hit. If you build tank, you deal 3% and take 30-45% per boss hit. Either way, the boss fight will take 60-90 minutes and will cycle through the same 3 mechanics. PRO TIP: enable "auto-victory" and click it often.

title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: After actually finishing the game. I think my review deserves a proper update. This game is something pretty special. It's a simple game, and I mean that in the best way. I took many 3 month breaks between sessions and didn't have any trouble transitioning back into actively playing. [h3] The Combat [/h3] is a mix of mega man battle network and paper mario. Though I've never touched either, I can say conceptually, it keeps combat fresh. The timing system, I found feels pretty forgiving, but it immediately humbled my naivety and growing complacency in the late game fights. Those last a WHILE and the damage is no joke if you fumble, definitely lead me to getting one-shot. The windows may be wide, but you're hurtling into bricks if you miss it. Also nice that there's just a run button to skip encounters because towards the end, I did not feel like fighting all that when it's just chump fights. I kinda dislike it "winning" fights sometimes but it doesn't count towards achievements so it was fine on that front, probably just an oversight. The combat also just has accessibility options which are always welcome if you don't want the stress of reflexes. But I really liked how the smaller encounters generally prepared you for each boss fight since a lot of concepts for moves are reused, so the flashier versions don't come out of nowhere. (With an exception of the final boss gauntlet but at that point it's just plain fun to supercede expectations). It's super satisfying to be able to use the whole catalogue of moves, except like, 2 that were pretty redundant. Since they all had different niche-use cases. Definitely adds replayability for minmaxers since you'd know bosses in advance. [h3] Exploration [/h3] The environments are well designed. All the secrets are fairly intuitive where I was only missing 2 out of the 4 dozen or so collectables. I only wish the gems were labelled individually (though there'd have to be an additional inventory menu to prevent clutter) to make backtracking less tedious. Some of the puzzles were pretty slack but not every dungeon is gonna be a banger in an rpg. That being said, every dungeon was unique and rich in colour and theming. This game also has a pretty effective horror atmosphere at times. I wouldn't call the game scary, but it's very believable when characters are supposed to be scared because the environment very much infers it. [h3] Plot [/h3] It's paced pretty well. It plays off the "3 friends in a magic school" trope and starts you off the aftermath of a [i]messy[/i] friend group. [i]Oh![/i] the drama is palpable. It's the kind of miscommunication plot I find entertaining because we find out all the withheld information with the characters that should've known it. Since we're seeing everything through Maritte, because she literally doesn't even go here. I think a neat touch is the pronouns on the party screen, I've never seen another game do it, letalone use neo-pronouns (My experience with it was I'd never been exposed to neo-pronouns before so I was confused by what was happening until I referenced the party screen after the conversation). And helps with the kind of subconcious profiling a player might do to identify a character by just laying it out as public knowledge. They don't give my girl Gilda enough screentime though. I'll let it slide because of the secret echoes fight kinda wraps all the character arcs up. [h3] Music/Animation/Sound Design [/h3] This was what got me into the game in the first place. I discovered Ikenfell from finding snippets of the album on Soundcloud and got hooked. I always find that I have the least to say in these sections of reviews because it always boils down to me saying "It's crunchy, it's cute, and I like watching the models spins around and stuff". Idk. I really like how this game is presented. (except the character portraits specifically, the cover banner and the album art are just superior renditions of the characters, but it doesn't take me out of it by any means). The animations compliment the combat beautifully and the impacts are tangible from the sound design on every piece of timing. I wish they used a few more tracks for chump encounters. But the soundtrack is solid. [b] Anyways everyone should play this. Took me about 30hrs to 100% it, and I loved every step.[/b]

title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: Really lovely little RPG, had a lot of fun and it's a solid little play. Story has a lot of nice little twists and revelations, for both characters and the overall plot. Characters are all largely likable and party members useful, equipment is mostly 'better number = better' but it does have a nice balance of choosing between some stats like stacking more defense or speed. Combat system is quite decent, though the ranges on abilities can be a little annoying at times and it gets a bit punishing later on, I ended up just turning off the button timing in combat (though you can leave it at 'everything is minimum good' for an okay challenge) Bosses can be a bit brutal with extra phases or they summon extra minions or a lot of enemies have multi hit abilities. Climax falls a little flat with an extra twist/revelation I don't think was explicitly needed and kind of takes away from the big fight before it. Final fight just feels kind of anticlimatic. Wonderful looking graphics, everything looks made with care and character and level design are well done. Wears it's queerness on it's sleeve, happy for the representation and treats everything as normal. Was a delight to see. Really hope to see more from this developer, this was an excellent little game and shows a lot of potential for more. Solid B+
